summary: MARTIAN MAP is a project we developed to explore the challenges of living and working on Mars. Our aim is to bring different tools for Martian exploration into one platform. It uses the Viking Orbiter Global Mosaic (MDIM) for surface imagery and MOLA MEGDR for elevation and terrain information. The project includes 14 modules covering astronaut survival, mission resource planning, habitat systems, EVA simulations, rover operations, terrain analysis, navigation and scientific exploration. We have also included archived MEDA observations from NASA's Perseverance rover and route analysis for the Jezero region. Users can explore Martian locations, view terrain information and test different mission scenarios. We have clearly separated actual scientific data from derived results and simulations. MARTIAN MAP is our attempt to make Mars exploration easier to understand and to support better preparation for future human missions.

MARTIAN MAP – INTERPLANETARY SURVIVAL GUIDE

1. INTRODUCTION

MARTIAN MAP is a Python-based Mars exploration and survival-support application developed to study different challenges involved in future human missions to Mars. The main idea behind this project is to bring Martian surface mapping, geographical information, terrain analysis, route planning and mission-support tools together in one platform.

Mars is an interesting planet for future exploration, but studying and exploring its surface involves many difficulties. Astronauts and robotic rovers need information about the surrounding terrain, possible routes, environmental conditions and available scientific observations before carrying out exploration activities.

To address these challenges, we developed MARTIAN MAP using available planetary datasets and Python programming. The application allows users to explore different Martian locations, understand elevation and slope variations, compare possible rover routes and examine simulated mission situations.

The project also includes scientific information from the Viking Orbiter Global Mosaic (MDIM), MOLA MEGDR and archived observations from the Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer (MEDA) on NASA's Perseverance rover.

Our aim is to create a single platform that makes Martian exploration and mission preparation easier to understand.

2. PROBLEM STATEMENT

Exploring Mars is difficult because of its unfamiliar surface, extreme environmental conditions, limited resources and communication challenges. Before planning an exploration mission, it is important to understand the geographical features of the selected region and identify terrain that may create difficulties for a rover or future explorers.

However, information about Mars is available through different scientific datasets, research platforms and analysis tools. Studying surface imagery, elevation, terrain conditions, archived observations and mission-related information separately can make the overall analysis difficult.

Another important challenge is that not all required environmental information is available in a single dataset. For example, elevation data alone cannot provide information about radiation, atmospheric pressure, water or mineral abundance.

Therefore, there is a need for an integrated platform that can bring available scientific information, terrain analysis and simulated mission-support functions together while clearly identifying missing or unavailable data.

MARTIAN MAP is developed to address this problem through a common interactive environment for Martian exploration and survival-related study.

3. MAIN AIM

The main aim of this project is to develop an interactive Mars exploration and survival-support system that helps users understand the Martian environment, analyse surface and terrain conditions, explore important locations and examine simulated exploration missions using available scientific datasets.

The project also aims to demonstrate how different scientific data sources and programming techniques can be combined to create a useful planetary exploration platform.

4. OBJECTIVES

The major objectives of MARTIAN MAP are:

1. To display and explore the global surface of Mars using scientific imagery and elevation datasets.

2. To study the geographical locations of important Martian landing sites and landforms.

3. To process elevation data and generate useful terrain information such as slope and roughness.

4. To compare possible rover exploration routes using distance and terrain-related information.

5. To provide a basic mission resource calculator for studying oxygen, water, food and energy requirements.

6. To demonstrate astronaut EVA and habitat monitoring through simulated values.

7. To display information about Mars orbiters and natural satellites.

8. To explore archived environmental observations collected by the Perseverance rover.

9. To identify scientific data gaps and distinguish measured information from derived results and simulations.

10. To bring different Martian exploration tools together through a common user interface.

5. DATASETS USED

The project uses planetary datasets as its scientific foundation. Each dataset has a specific purpose in the application.

5.1 Viking Orbiter Global Mosaic (MDIM)

The Viking Orbiter Global Mosaic is used as the global surface imagery source for Mars. It provides visual information about the planet's surface and helps users understand the distribution of major geographical features.

In the desktop application, the processed Viking imagery is used as the texture for the 3D Mars globe. It also supports the global surface mapping feature.

5.2 MOLA MEGDR

The Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) dataset provides global elevation information about the Martian surface.

The project uses MOLA MEGDR elevation data to create global topographic grids. This information is also used to generate a reduced-resolution elevation grid for the 3D globe.

The elevation data helps identify higher and lower regions, large geographical variations and general surface characteristics.

5.3 Jezero Crater CTX Digital Elevation Model

A regional Context Camera (CTX) Digital Elevation Model with approximately 20-metre grid spacing is used for Jezero Crater analysis.

This dataset provides more detailed regional elevation information than the global elevation grid. It is used to generate slope and roughness layers and supports experimental terrain-cost calculations and route comparisons.

5.4 MEDA Archived Observations

The Mars Environmental Dynamics Analyzer (MEDA) is an instrument on NASA's Perseverance rover.

The project includes archived MEDA ATS CSV files from selected mission sols, including Sol 1 and Sol 1740. These files contain instrument observation records that can be explored through charts and tables.

The ATS_ATS1 to ATS_ATS5 channels are displayed as raw engineering counts. They are not directly treated as calibrated temperatures or weather measurements.

6. METHOD AND WORKING PROCEDURE

The project follows a data-driven development approach. The major steps involved are explained below.

Step 1: Data Collection

The required Mars datasets are collected from planetary science data sources. The Viking MDIM dataset is used for global imagery, MOLA MEGDR for elevation and the Jezero CTX DEM for regional terrain study.

Archived MEDA observations are also included for scientific data exploration.

Step 2: Data Processing

Python and NumPy are used to read and process the collected datasets.

The original MOLA elevation data is available at a much higher resolution. To make it easier to visualise and process, the project generates reduced-resolution grids.

A 4-pixel-per-degree global elevation grid is generated for global terrain analysis. A separate 360 × 180 elevation grid is produced for the 3D globe.

Step 3: Terrain Analysis

Elevation data is used to calculate surface slope. Slope represents how quickly the elevation changes across neighbouring locations.

The Jezero regional elevation model is also used to generate roughness information. Roughness helps describe local variations in the terrain surface.

These parameters are useful for comparing different areas, especially when studying possible rover exploration routes.

Step 4: Terrain-Cost Calculation

The project combines normalised slope and roughness information to generate an experimental relative terrain-cost index.

The terrain-cost calculation uses a weighted combination of these two parameters. Higher relative cost values indicate terrain that is less preferred by the experimental route-planning model.

This index is used for route comparison and is not a validated rover mobility or safety score.

Step 5: Route Planning

The project uses the A* pathfinding algorithm to identify possible paths through a regional terrain-cost grid.

The algorithm considers the cost of moving between neighbouring grid cells and searches for a lower-cost path between the selected starting and ending points.

Different route candidates are compared, including:

• Shortest-distance route.

• Balanced terrain route.

• Terrain-cost-avoiding route.

These routes help demonstrate how terrain conditions can influence exploration planning.

Step 6: Application Development

The desktop application is developed using Python and PySide6. Different pages are connected through a common navigation system.

NumPy is used for numerical calculations, Rasterio for raster data handling, Pillow for image processing and Matplotlib for scientific visualisations.

A browser version has also been developed using Streamlit and Plotly to make the project accessible through a public web link.

7. PROJECT MODEL AND WORKING EXPLANATION

MARTIAN MAP is organised into different modules. Each module performs a particular task, but together they form an integrated Mars exploration environment.

7.1 Mars Mapping

The Mars mapping section provides a global view of the planet.

The 3D globe combines Viking surface imagery and MOLA elevation-based topography in the desktop version. Users can rotate and zoom the globe and explore important Martian locations.

The application includes locations such as Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Gusev Crater, Meridiani Planum, Olympus Mons and Valles Marineris.

7.2 Terrain Intelligence

This section focuses on understanding the surface characteristics of Mars.

It includes elevation, slope and roughness information for the Jezero region. Users can select different terrain layers and examine their variations through visualisations.

The relative terrain-cost layer combines slope and roughness information to support experimental route planning.

7.3 Route Planning and Mars Navigation

The project provides two different types of route-related analysis.

The first is global geographical distance calculation using the great-circle method. It estimates the shortest distance between two selected Martian locations based on the mean radius of Mars.

The second is regional terrain-cost-based route planning for Jezero Crater. It uses the A* algorithm to compare possible routes while considering terrain cost.

These two methods serve different purposes. Great-circle distance is a geometric estimate, while the Jezero route candidates use regional terrain information.

7.4 Mission Support

The mission-support section contains tools that demonstrate different aspects of future human exploration.

The Mission Twin allows users to configure crew size, mission duration and available supplies. It calculates the estimated oxygen, water, food and energy requirements using editable demonstration consumption rates.

Habitat Systems displays resource reserves and conceptual subsystem information.

The Astronaut EVA module demonstrates spacesuit-related parameters such as oxygen, battery, carbon dioxide, temperature, humidity and heart rate through simulated telemetry.

7.5 Rover Operations

The Rover Operations module demonstrates the movement of a simulated rover along selected Jezero route candidates.

It displays information such as simulated speed, battery, pitch, roll, heading, distance and mission progress.

The route selection feature allows users to examine different precomputed route candidates and understand how a rover exploration scenario could be represented digitally.

7.6 Orbital Operations

The Orbital Assets module provides information about spacecraft associated with Mars exploration.

The project includes Mars Odyssey, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Express, ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter, Emirates Mars Mission Hope and Tianwen-1 Orbiter.

It also displays the natural satellites Phobos and Deimos.

The orbital paths and moving markers are schematic visual representations. They are not live spacecraft positions or real-time orbital calculations.

7.7 Scientific Information and Discovery

The scientific modules help users examine available datasets and understand where additional information is required.

Resource Intelligence presents the available terrain evidence and identifies missing water, ice and mineral-composition measurements.

Unknown Frontier highlights information gaps such as radiation dose, calibrated atmospheric pressure, temperature, water and mineral evidence.

Martian Science Lab provides a summary of available datasets, grid dimensions, sampled numerical statistics and scientific visualisations.

MEDA Observations allows users to select archived datasets and ATS channels, view observation charts and inspect a preview of the recorded data.

8. DESCRIPTION OF THE 14 APPLICATION MODULES

The application contains 14 modules arranged into five major groups.

A. Overview

1. Command Centre

This is the main page of the application. It provides the Mars globe, global data information, named Martian locations and mission route endpoint selection. It acts as the starting point for exploring the other modules.

B. Survival Systems

2. Survival Guide

Provides an evidence-based overview of possible Martian mission challenges. It identifies available scientific information and missing environmental measurements.

3. Mission Twin

Allows users to configure a simulated mission by changing crew size, mission duration and available resources. It calculates estimated resource consumption and remaining supplies.

4. Habitat Systems

Displays conceptual habitat subsystem information and resource reserves. It connects with the Mission Twin demonstration results.

5. Astronaut EVA

Provides a simulated spacesuit monitoring interface. It displays oxygen, battery, CO₂, temperature, humidity and heart-rate values.

C. Field Operations

6. Rover Operations

Demonstrates simulated rover movement along precomputed Jezero route candidates and displays basic telemetry-style information.

7. Mars Environment

Provides global scientific map layers, including elevation and slope, along with information about important Martian locations.

8. Terrain Intelligence

Displays Jezero regional elevation, slope, roughness and relative terrain-cost information. It also supports experimental A* route planning in the original desktop application.

9. Mars Nav

Calculates geographical distance between selected Martian locations using the great-circle method and helps define route endpoints.

D. Orbital Operations

10. Orbital Assets

Displays information about selected Mars orbiters and the natural satellites Phobos and Deimos. It includes schematic orbital visualisations.

E. Science and Discovery

11. Resource Intelligence

Presents available terrain evidence and identifies the limitations of the current data when studying possible water, ice and mineral resources.

12. Unknown Frontier

Displays scientific information that is currently unavailable, uncalibrated or not verified by the datasets used in the project.

13. Martian Science Lab

Provides dataset information, sampled numerical statistics and visualisations of global and regional terrain products.

14. MEDA Observations

Provides access to archived MEDA ATS data. Users can select a dataset and channel, view the observation graph and inspect sample records.

9. SOFTWARE AND TECHNOLOGIES USED

The project uses the following programming languages and software libraries:

• Python: Main programming language used for application development and data processing.

• PySide6: Used to develop the original desktop graphical user interface.

• Streamlit: Used to create the browser-based version of the application.

• NumPy: Used for numerical calculations, array processing and terrain analysis.

• Rasterio: Used for reading and handling geographical raster datasets.

• Pillow: Used for image processing and resizing.

• Matplotlib: Used to generate scientific charts and visualisations in the desktop application.

• Plotly: Used for interactive 3D visualisation and charts in the browser version.

• A Algorithm:* Used for experimental terrain-cost-based route planning.

• GitHub: Used for source-code storage and version management.

• Streamlit Community Cloud: Used to host the public browser application.

10. RESULTS AND EXPECTED OUTPUT

The project brings together different tools required for studying Martian exploration in one application.

The main outputs include:

1. A global Mars globe and geographical location explorer.

2. Global MOLA elevation and derived slope visualisations.

3. Regional Jezero elevation, slope and roughness previews.

4. Experimental terrain-cost and route comparison outputs.

5. Great-circle distance calculations between selected Martian locations.

6. Simulated mission resource calculations.

7. Simulated astronaut EVA and habitat monitoring.

8. Rover route visualisation and simulated mission progress.

9. Orbital asset information and schematic orbit visualisations.

10. Archived MEDA observation charts and data previews.

11. Scientific data availability and limitation reports.

Through these outputs, users can understand how planetary datasets can be processed and combined to support exploration and mission-preparation activities.

11. LIMITATIONS OF THE PROJECT

MARTIAN MAP is a research and educational prototype. Some features are based on available scientific data, while other features are demonstrations created to explain possible mission scenarios.

The Mission Twin uses editable demonstration consumption rates and does not represent approved life-support engineering calculations.

The EVA and Habitat Systems modules use simulated values. They are not connected to real astronaut equipment, sensors or spacecraft hardware.

Rover movement and telemetry are simulated. The route candidates are experimental and should not be treated as certified rover commands.

The orbital paths and animated spacecraft markers are schematic and do not represent real-time ephemeris.

MEDA ATS values are archived raw engineering counts. They require the correct calibration information before they can be interpreted as physical measurements such as temperature.

The current browser deployment uses MOLA elevation relief, but the reduced Viking MDIM web texture has not yet been added. Some large regional Jezero arrays are also excluded from the lightweight web deployment, so certain advanced terrain calculations available in the original desktop project are not currently available online.

The application does not directly establish radiation exposure, atmospheric conditions, water or ice abundance, mineral composition or human habitability from the two global mapping datasets.

Therefore, the system should be considered an exploration and learning platform rather than a certified astronaut safety or operational mission-planning system.

12. FUTURE SCOPE

The project can be improved further by adding more scientific datasets and developing additional interactive features.

Possible future improvements include:

1. Integrating the reduced Viking MDIM texture into the browser version to provide the same textured 3D globe as the desktop application.

2. Adding more regional high-resolution terrain datasets for other important Martian locations.

3. Integrating properly calibrated environmental observations from NASA's Mars missions.

4. Adding dedicated scientific evidence layers for radiation, water ice and mineral composition.

5. Improving terrain-cost calculations using additional terrain parameters.

6. Developing more detailed rover simulation and route evaluation features.

7. Integrating verified spacecraft ephemeris data instead of schematic orbital paths.

8. Improving the browser interface to provide closer functional similarity to the desktop application.

9. Adding more interactive scientific charts and downloadable analysis reports.

10. Expanding the platform for future mission studies and educational use.

13. CONCLUSION

MARTIAN MAP is an attempt to combine planetary mapping, scientific data processing, terrain analysis and mission-support demonstrations into a single Mars exploration platform.

Through Viking imagery, MOLA elevation data, Jezero regional terrain products and archived MEDA observations, the project provides different ways to understand the Martian surface and available scientific information.

The 14 modules make it possible to explore Martian locations, compare terrain, examine route candidates, calculate simulated mission resources and study different aspects of astronaut and rover operations.

One of the important aspects of this project is that it separates actual scientific datasets, derived results, archived measurements and simulated information. This helps users understand what the available data can support and what still requires further research.

Overall, MARTIAN MAP demonstrates how Python programming, scientific datasets, numerical analysis and interactive visualisation can be brought together to support the study of future human exploration on Mars.
